items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Jack Dorsey’s Block is cutting jobs again. Here’s what makes these layoffs different
items.content_html:
Jack Dorsey’s fintech company, Block, began a second round of layoffs on Wednesday, months after cutting more than 4,000 jobs in February. The company has not said how many employees are affected at this time. 

The cuts hit the Customer Ops, Risk Ops, and Learning & Content Operations teams supporting Cash App, Block’s consumer financial services app, and Square, its tool for sellers. According to Business Insider, those teams will be “reducing the number of roles, changing some responsibilities, and shifting some reporting lines.” 

Affected employees are expected to receive a “separation package and transition support, similar to those affected in February 2026.” Block has not detailed the new terms. In February, laid-off employees received 20 weeks or more of severance pay, with the final amount dependent on tenure. Their packages also included equity vested until the end of May, six months of healthcare coverage, their company-issued work devices, and an extra $5,000.

Block did not respond to Fast Company’s request for comment as of publication. 

The layoffs came one day after Block reported its third-quarter results on Tuesday. The company said it raised its 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, up from its initial $12.51 billion estimate. It also projected a fourth-quarter gross profit of $3.32 billion. 

Block hasn’t explained what drove this round of layoffs. Earlier this year, Dorsey announced that the February layoffs were not because of financial issues, but because of “intelligence tools,” like AI.

“A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better,” Dorsey wrote on X then. “Intelligence tool capabilities are compounding faster every week.”

“We see an opportunity to move faster with smaller, highly talented teams using AI to automate more work,” Block CFO Amrita Ahuja said. 

Block is also continuing to build its own AI products. The company recently released Dessa, a speech-to-speech AI voice model trained on the recording of real human conversations.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Anthropic’s AI development has doubled in speed despite slowdown calls, research group says
items.content_html:
Anthropic is developing its artificial intelligence systems around twice as quickly as it was a year ago amid the CEO’s calls to slow down the technology’s pace of improvement, according to an analysis released Thursday by an independent monitoring group.

Anthropic invited researchers from the Berkeley, California-based nonprofit, Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), to review its internal data and interview staff as it prepares for its Wall Street debut with debate swirling over the potential for AI models to elude human control with catastrophic consequences.

The findings are significant because details about the technology—and its risks—have been provided primarily by AI companies, which have been encouraged by President Donald Trump’s administration to police themselves on matters of safety.

It was during the research group’s assessment period that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the AI industry to slow its work so safety measures can catch up. In a September 12 essay responding to mounting concerns about runaway AI, he urged the AI world to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.”

Anthropic did not immediately comment on the report in response to inquiries.

The San Francisco-based company is planning to go public later this month in what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever.

AI is playing a bigger role in its own improvement

METR estimated that Anthropic is improving the capabilities of its models to do “well-specified tasks” around twice as fast as it was a year earlier. The nonprofit’s researchers said they believed much of the reason for the faster development is the help of AI itself.

Anthropic has said its Claude chatbot is increasingly helping the company develop newer, more advanced versions of itself.

METR has conducted evaluations on model capabilities for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other labs for years. The nonprofit is funded through donations and does not accept compensation for its work, but AI companies it has partnered with for evaluations have provided access and tokens, which METR uses for evaluations, research, and engineering.

One of its two reports was based on analysis of Anthropic’s internal data provided by the company over a period of about 11 weeks, from mid-August through late October, as well as employee interviews.

METR said its assessment focused on two questions: whether the growth rate of Anthropic’s internal capabilities has accelerated and how much of that was attributable to AI. The group said it was given “unprecedented access to internal data” on Anthropic’s AI research and development process.

Anthropic’s redactions to the report limited how METR could communicate more detailed estimates of acceleration, and there were some internal disagreements and uncertainty among METR’s team, but the group said it believed the company’s rate of improvement had doubled.

“Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025,” according to the METR report.

METR also reviewed both a public risk report Anthropic published in August and a private version, as well as other non-public data, and the organization said the public report “overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring.”

Assessors see little holding back AI’s progress

The report was peppered with caveats. METR said it could be overstating its findings, because the acceleration might only be limited to “well-specified tasks” that can be graded automatically or with a language model, instead of “messy” tasks that are harder to define. Or it could be that Anthropic understated its previous progress, making the latest number look bigger.

METR said it was able to “confidently” rule out the growth of computing power used in training AI models as the reason for the acceleration. Traditionally, the amount of computing power, known as compute, is directly related to how well an AI model performs. The researchers said their guess was that the improvement was down to using AI itself to improve AI.

A key concern, METR said, is that using AI to improve itself could start to compound the acceleration, which could be especially worrying given that researchers found there were no “bottlenecks” such as restrictions on computing power or data holding back Anthropic’s AI progress.

“We understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model-training process,” the report said. However, Anthropic researchers described significant “signs of life” implying that could happen soon, METR said.

Amodei touched on this issue in his September essay, saying AI advances have been driven primarily by the concept of recursive self-improvement, or what he defined as “AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI.”

“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” Amodei wrote.

In that same essay, Amodei championed the idea of having external evaluators embedded within the leading AI labs and specifically highlighted METR as an appropriate third-party evaluator. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said at the time that he also supported the idea of independent evaluators with employee-like access.

—By Kelvin Chan and Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press

items.title: Pluralistic: Without CDA 230, Facebook will own the internet forever (05 Nov 2026)
items.content_html: Today's links Without CDA 230, Facebook will own the internet forever: Small, well-managed online communities are especially vulnerable to legal threats. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: "Perfect Thing"; Recruiters tell students Iraq war is over; Toothpick Final Fantasy replicas; "Eleanor & Park"; Voter Suppression Trail; "Science Comics Computers." Upcoming appearances: Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Without CDA 230, Facebook will own the internet forever (permalink) The road to hell is paved with the depraved indifference to badly considered tech policy. The internet is one of those charismatic hyperobjects that wraps around our lives in myriad ways, so tech policy changes have a big blast radius. This isn't a counsel of despair. I firmly believe that we can make tech policy, and furthermore, that we must, but that policy has to be crafted in a way that's mindful of collateral damage. Take scraping. Most creative workers are rightly furious at the palpable glee of tech bosses, who want to take everything we've made in order to train models whose express purpose is to destroy our livelihoods and transfer our wages to AI companies and the media companies they sell to. This is an entirely correct thing to be angry about. But many of my peers and comrades think the answer to this is to ban scraping, which is a terrible idea. Scraping is how we make search engines. If you want Google to be the last search engine we ever get then by all means, change the rules so you need licenses to make transient copies of the web. There's only one company with deep-enough pockets to secure permission from every web site operator: Google, the thrice-convicted monopolist that dominates the web so thoroughly that no one could afford to turn them down. Scraping is how we glue down the web's shifting sands. If you want to understand why the web says something today, it helps to know what it said yesterday. If we want to know how Zuck and Musk's algorithms are peddling disinformation and hatred, we need to be able to scrape their feeds. If we want to know how Amazon uses surveillance data to price-gouge shoppers, we need to scrape its prices. If we want to know how Uber cheats its most economically desperate drivers with lowball wage offers, we need to scrape its job listings. (It's possible to make a scraper that's so clumsy or aggressive that it crashes or destroys websites. That's a dick move. We should find people who do that and punish them; and the thing we should punish them for is trashing websites – not making transient copies of the data on those sites.) (If you want to protect creative livelihoods from AI bosses, the answer lies in labor organizing, not more copyright:) https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/21/off-the-menu/#universally-loathed The point is that while tech bosses are some of the worst, most eminently guillotineable monsters history has produced, tech is important to the lives of billions of perfectly nice people. If you let your rage at tech bosses overwhelm your care for those everyday people, you risk coming up with "punishments" that end up benefiting Big Tech and wrecking the lives of those normal users. For example: you may have heard people insist that we can solve our problems with Big Tech by "repealing Section 230." This is a reference to section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 26-word law that makes users responsible for their speech, while insulating the platforms that facilitate that speech from liability: https://www.techdirt.com/2020/06/23/hello-youve-been-referred-here-because-youre-wrong-about-section-230-communications-decency-act/ Here's what that means: say one user accuses another user of violating their rights through their words (libelling them, invading their privacy, etc). The wronged party can sue the person they're accusing of harming them, but they can't sue the social media platform, message board provider, hosting company, DNS provider (etc etc) for their role in hosting and transmitting the unlawful speech. At the same time, CDA 230 allows all these "intermediaries" (social media platforms, hosting companies, message board providers, etc etc) to take down or otherwise moderate content that they deem offensive, without creating an obligation to police all of their users' speech. CDA 230 grew out of lawsuits in the 1990s where online companies that took any action to remove offensive or unlawful speech were thereafter obliged to take down all unlawful speech. The lawfulness or unlawfulness of speech isn't something you can easily determine: for example, determining whether one user libeled another user requires that you find out whether the allegedly libelous speech is true. There's no way that a forum moderator can know that – it's the kind of thing you need a judge, a jury and a trial to figure out. The result of these lawsuits was that most platforms decided they wouldn't take down any speech (so as to avoid creating an obligation to police all user speech), while a minority of platforms simply removed anything that anyone might find offensive. It was a mess: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratton_Oakmont,_Inc._v._Prodigy_Services_Co. CDA 230 fixed that. CDA 230 is how an individual or a small organization can host its own Mastodon or Bluesky servers, its own message boards, etc. It's these "smallhosts" that are the primary beneficiaries of CDA 230, not the Big Tech companies that 230's opponents hope to target by reforming or repealing 230. Big Tech would be happy to see CDA 230 repealed. Mark Zuckerberg has repeatedly called for CDA 230 to be deleted, because he thinks that Meta could hire enough moderators (or use enough AI) that they could avoid being ensnared in a lot of frivolous litigation, and when legal threats did land, Zuck's army of lawyers could readily see them off: https://cepr.net/publications/repealing-section-230-giving-mark-zuckerberg-what-he-wants/ Big Tech's biggest fear isn't a repeal of CDA 230: it's mass defection of its users to smaller, independent services that are more responsive to users' needs. Zuck doesn't care if we get a new law that would make it impossible for another #MeToo to take off! This is on my mind this week because of the way that intermediary liability has nearly destroyed an online community that I helped found, way back in the early 1990s. The community is a small arts organization that I joined as a teenager. The organization sent out a quarterly newsletter, which I devoured as soon as it arrived in my mailbox. I wanted more! A few years in, I had the idea of setting up an email list for the org. Another member had access to a server where we could host the list, and now, more than 30 years later, that list is still going strong. Now, every small community has its cranks and trolls, and this one is no exception. One member in particular has a well-earned reputation for flying off the handle, showering anyone who disagrees with them with furious and obscene abuse (I've been on the receiving end of this abuse myself). Unsurprisingly, this person is also an inveterate culture warrior who can be relied upon to troll anyone who brings up racial or gender issues. When this trolling draws the inevitable critical response, this person then reverts to form, showering their critics with abuse and profanity. The list is moderated, and the organization's code of conduct is used as a framework for the moderators' calls. Like most codes of conduct, this org's CoC includes some generalities that leave room for interpretation (basically, "Don't be a dick"). A moderation policy that allows the moderators to sanction users for flaming each other and a user who picks fights and then launches into unhinged tirades at the mildest of criticisms were always going to collide, and that's what happened with this user. After picking a fight over racist language, this user posted a bunch of racial epithets and got sanctioned for posting racist language. That's when the user sued the organization's volunteer board members for libel for implying that they were racist, seeking tens of thousands of dollars in damages, far in excess of the org's cash reserves. The org stepped in to defend its board members, and even though this trollish member quickly folded their legal threat, mounting just that initial defense incinerated a sizable fraction of the org's total assets. This is the thing that CDA 230 was designed to prevent. Even spurious legal threats can wipe out small, volunteer-run communities. In the 30 years since I founded this list, there have been a couple times when members tried to convince the organization to move it to Facebook or another Big Tech platform. Each time, the rest of us were able to rebuff those efforts, and today the list continues to be independently operated. If this one belligerent jerk had held out for just a little longer, that would have been the end of this community – not just the mailing list, but the organization itself. We can't have an indieweb without limited liability for intermediaries. Repealing CDA 230 won't hurt Facebook – it will just force every independent community to move there. items.title: [wsj.com] OpenAI weighs capacity reset as voters curb data-center growth
items.content_html: OpenAI leaders discussed Wednesday whether election results should prompt the company to revise its data-center capacity expectations for next year, as restrictions threaten facilities that supply computing power for AI training and services. In the Nov. 3 midterms, voters backed data-center limits in all but one of 41 local ballot contests tracked by Ballotpedia and CNBC, while Democrats won Congress and governorships in major data-center states. The local votes could affect projects on different schedules. A planned Ohio campus secured by OpenAI calls for 8 gigawatts of computing capacity, with the first phase of construction slated to begin this year and capacity expected to come online starting in 2028. Analysts say restrictions are more likely to slow future projects than facilities already under construction or approved through 2027. Democrats have called for AI company executives to testify and for investigations, while some newly elected lawmakers have proposed AI safety reviews and new oversight structures. The new Congress is due to convene on Jan. 3, 2027.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Google announces it will cut off internet search access for schools that reject AI
items.content_html:
Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to using artificial intelligence, the tech giant said Tuesday.

The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.

On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators. Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off — including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search, with each being off by default until administrators turn it on. But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.

“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.

The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.”

But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.

Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.

Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.

Tuesday’s announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers.

“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.

Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development.

Josh Golin, executive director of children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said Google’s attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google’s technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.

“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.

Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

—Barbara Ortutay, AP Technology Writer

items.title: [cybersecuritydive.com] Companies increase cybersecurity budgets as unapproved AI escapes oversight

About 74.5% reported larger budgets than a year earlier, and 40.3% said their next security dollar would go to AI security and governance; 46.1% said an employee had connected an unapproved AI tool to a company environment, while 20.1% reported a resulting security incident. The attack requires a retry of a failed download and manipulation of HTTP traffic; Debian and Ubuntu enable retries by default on some newer releases. Debian fixed the bug in APT 3.0.4 for Trixie and 2.6.2 for Bookworm. Ubuntu published patched builds for releases from 22.04 through 26.10 and listed fixes for older releases under extended support. Administrators are advised to install the vendor update; Ubuntu’s instructions disable retries for the update command as a temporary safeguard.

items.content_html: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say attackers are hijacking companies’ access to large language models (LLMs), running up unauthorized cloud charges of more than $100,000 in a day and up to $1 million before access is cut off. Their report, based on incidents investigated in 2026, describes criminals using stolen cloud credentials and AI API keys to run models or resell access, leaving affected organizations with the bills. The attacks have affected organizations in financial services, retail, technology and transportation across North America, South America and Asia-Pacific. Google says attackers often gain access through exposed or stolen identity tokens, then sell that access through illicit routing services known as LLM Mixers. One such service, Jet Night, advertised unlimited access for about $60 a month. Google recommends tighter access controls, centralized management of secrets and monitoring for unauthorized AI use and unusual spending.

items.title: [therecord.media] XCPE botnet included 32,532 Android devices in Turkey, report says
items.content_html: Figures from TrendAI cited by Turkish technology site DonanımHaber identified 32,532 devices in Turkey linked to XCPE, an Android-device botnet. Google says Shenzhen-based manufacturer Videostrong Technology deliberately backdoored the hardware and sold access to criminal affiliates. Turkey ranked 11th among affected countries in TrendAI’s count. Google and security partners, working with Japan’s National Police Agency, disrupted the botnet’s control infrastructure. The devices’ residential-proxy modules routed outside traffic through owners’ home internet connections, making victims’ IP addresses appear to be the source of activity. Other modules enabled advertising fraud and the installation of additional malware. TrendAI’s Robert McArdle said criminals could use affected households’ and businesses’ connections without their knowledge, including for attacks that impersonate people in their region. TrendAI recorded more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation from June 3 to Oct. 1. That figure measures observed addresses, not infected devices. The takedown cut command links but did not remove the firmware backdoor. Synthient advised owners to replace affected devices, while security guidance also recommends disconnecting suspect boxes and changing potentially exposed Wi-Fi passwords.

items.title: [therecord.media] UK food suppliers report refrigeration hacks as cyber agency warns of risks
items.content_html: Three British meat suppliers and a fruit-and-vegetable wholesaler said intruders remotely changed settings on their internet-connected refrigeration controls during the Nov. 2 attacks across Europe. The meat suppliers said they lost no stock, and the wholesaler said staff disconnected a unit before its produce spoiled. The incidents remain unattributed, and no group has claimed responsibility. The three meat suppliers said attackers accessed Copeland XWEB supervisory controllers. A security notice said versions 1.12.1 and earlier contained severe authentication-bypass flaws that could allow control without a password; firmware updates had been available since August. Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the government’s cyber defense agency, said it worked through the night to contact organizations with vulnerable systems exposed to the internet. NCSC chief executive Richard Horne described the national impact as minimal but said the consequences for affected businesses and their employees could be severe. The agency’s annual report warned that organizations were failing to implement basic cyber protections, and its director of operations said the attacks used known vulnerabilities rather than sophisticated techniques.

items.title: [simonwillison.net] MIT researchers show AI can edit neural network weights directly
items.content_html: MIT researchers reported that OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra can inspect and directly alter another neural network’s weights without gradient-based retraining, a technique they call “Weight-Space Programming”. In tests, Astra changed 0.016% of Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to address reasoning loops; the model’s MATH-500 score rose from 7.9% to 48.1%, while its GSM8K and IFEval scores also increased. The team also reported that Astra identified small game-playing networks by examining their weights and generated networks for games including Breakout, without training data or gradient updates. The researchers tested small models and networks and said they are developing a benchmark and testing framework. Independent experiments found that some other language models can interpret game-network weights, while commentators have questioned whether the findings demonstrate a general understanding of weights.

items.title: [cyberscoop.com] Google disrupts 1.3 million-device botnet used for global proxy traffic
items.content_html: The XCPE botnet infected devices in more than 170 countries, with the largest concentrations in Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan. TrendAI counted 1,472,554 infected devices across 206 models from June 3 to Oct. 1, 2026. Nearly 44,000 infected devices were in the United States. Google and security partners disrupted the network, which relied on a backdoor embedded in devices made by Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology, and took down control domains used by more than a dozen related malware families. Criminal affiliates used the set-top boxes to run advertising fraud, sell access to household internet connections through residential proxy networks and install additional malware. Google estimates that taking down affiliate control domains could sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices infected by other routes; that estimate is separate from XCPE’s 1.3 million-plus devices. Deleting the malware’s app does not remove the firmware backdoor, which can reinstall the app after a reboot. Google says owners need clean firmware or should disconnect affected devices from the internet; researchers have also urged organizations to identify and isolate suspect devices on their networks.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Hackers may have found a surprising new target: Your grocery store’s frozen food aisle
items.content_html:
Grocery stores across Europe faced an overnight cyberattack on Monday, affecting the refrigerated and freezer sections and leading to product losses.

The new wave of cyberattacks affected grocery stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, and Estonia, Reuters previously reported..The attacks took place overnight, raising the temperatures both freezer and refrigerator units to 122 degrees Fahrenheit resulting in widespread food spoilage and some units catching fire.

The attacks affected major retailers across the continent including stores owned by Ahold Delhaize, Colruyt, ICA and Coop.  IKEA—which also sells frozen food including its iconic meatballs—also confirmed to Fast Company that one location in Mons, Belgium has also been affected.

“Our teams are investigating to better understand the nature and scope of the incident and any potential impact on our operations. We are also carrying out precautionary checks across our markets,” an IKEA spokesperson told Fast Company.

Fast Company also reached out to Ahold Delhaize, Colruyt, ICA and IKEA for comment but did not receive a response by publication time.

Coop confirmed to Fast Company that around seven of 800 Sweden locations were affected by the attack, with issues ranging from complete refrigerator and freezer shutdowns to partially functioning equipment, and one instance of a system generating heat. According to Carlos Cancino, head of press relations at Coop Sweden, the affected locations are now fully operational again.

The incidents follow a similar cyberattack in France last month, which affected around 700 grocery stores with losses estimated at tens of millions of euros. The attacks, which also raised the freezer and refrigerator system’s temperature to around 122 degrees, caused loss of food and some fires.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it—a warning that we must take seriously,” EU commissioner for agriculture, Christophe Hansen, told Reuters. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning.”

The widespread attacks have been possible due to technologies that allow for remote controlling in-store systems from freezers to surveillance cameras. Both attacks seem to have compromised internet-connected units using mostly temperature control technology from Danish engineering company Danfoss.

The attacks point to growing vulnerabilities in the food supply chain. Last year, United Natural Foods (UNFI) faced “unauthorized activity” on its IT systems, with grocery stores across the country experiencing disruptions as a result from the attacks.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI and women at work: 5 positives, 8 negatives
items.content_html:
The debate about AI and work often focuses on the jobs that will disappear, which tasks will be automated, and which skills and qualities will be valued in the future. Seldom do I read articles that analyze the impact of AI on exhaustion and pleasure at work. And those questions are usually asked about “workers” in general, as if the answers were the same for men and women. There are many reasons why they are not. Because women and men are concentrated in different occupations, perform different tasks within the same organizations, and are judged differently for the same work, artificial intelligence affects women’s work in very specific ways.

Is the overall effect positive or negative? It isn’t easy to say, so I made an old-fashioned list of pros and cons, the kind people draw up when deciding whether to change jobs or leave a relationship. I ended up with more negatives than positives: five reasons to be hopeful and eight reasons to worry.


On the hopeful side

1. Today’s job growth is happening mostly in women’s jobs, and they aren’t very much exposed to AI. In 2025, healthcare and social assistance accounted for almost all net job creation in the U.S.—about 405,000 jobs in healthcare and 308,000 in social assistance. If it weren’t for those two sectors, the U.S. would have lost jobs last year. The Bureau of Labor Statistics anticipates that this will continue to be the case in the coming decade because of population aging. We will need a lot of caregivers in the future, and large language models (LLMs) can’t take their place. That protects women’s employment, but it does little for their pay: Care work remains poorly compensated, and in the U.S. its growth also depends on public money that hinges on political choices. The coming midterm elections will say a lot about where things are heading.

2. AI could make “greedy jobs” less hostile to women. A big part of the pay gap is attributable to the unequal distribution of the highest-paying jobs. The so-called “greedy jobs” reward presenteeism and excessive workloads, which penalizes everyone who can’t give work all of their time. In law, finance, consulting, or medicine, value is tied to being the one person who knows the client or the case. If AI makes expertise portable, making a client’s or a case’s history immediately accessible to other colleagues, then it could reduce the premium on being irreplaceable. This is what digital records did to the pharmacy industry, which went from a male-dominated, unequal profession in 1970s America to an equal one. Of course, we’ll still need employers to decide to redesign those jobs, and that can never be guaranteed. 

3. Hurrah, some of the most tedious office chores are now being automated. Writing meeting minutes, taking notes, organizing schedules, drafting follow-up emails: Most of these “non-promotable tasks” are important but do nothing to advance the career of those who do them. And they fall predominantly on women’s shoulders. (That shouldn’t come as a surprise: They’re exactly like household chores.) The time spent on them could be spent on more visible tasks that can earn you a promotion. So AI tools that automate them are more than welcome! Likewise, there’s less paperwork in care jobs. Nurses and doctors are worn down by paperwork. Using AI tools can help them focus more on patients, which happens to be the part of the job they like best.

4. The barriers to entrepreneurship and to building with tech are lower now. Women who start companies have always had to do more with less. In the U.S., startups founded only by women still get roughly 2% of venture capital (and this share isn’t budging). AI makes it possible to start small and still go far. On your own, you can accomplish so much more with an army of “agents”! You can create a website with very little money, draft contracts, and answer customers. According to equity management platform Carta, the share of new startups with a single founder rose from about 24% in 2019 to 36% in the first half of 2025. AI-assisted coding also enables people to develop digital tools without knowing how to code, which is remarkable in a field where women are in the minority. 

5. Relational skills are gaining value. As AI takes over the codifiable part of cognitive work, the value of what it doesn’t do so well could go up: coordinating, caring, and exercising judgment in context. A lot of women have acquired these skills through decades of being expected to look after others and manage their emotions. If AI does raise the value of those skills, the market may have to pay more for them and stop seeing them as “naturally” feminine and therefore of little value. 

On the worrisome side

1. The most exposed white-collar jobs are disproportionately held by women. In rich countries, according to the International Labour Organization, 9.6% of women’s jobs fall into the highest category of exposure to generative AI, compared with 3.5% of men’s jobs. The reason is that women are concentrated in clerical jobs: assistants, secretaries, and payroll and data entry clerks. Not all these jobs will disappear. But we already have an idea of how they can change. Translation is a mostly female profession (around 7 in 10 translators and interpreters in the U.S. are women). A big share of translators have lost work to generative AI (and others have changed professions already). Many of those who still have work now spend their days editing machine output, for less money. 

2. The first rungs of the ladder are disappearing. For generations, junior administrative and clerical jobs were a route into employment, as well as upward mobility, for women without higher education. A secretary could become an office manager, then an executive assistant, then an operations manager. If AI eliminates most of these entry points, the career ladder gets cut at the bottom—and that’s bad news for women.

3. Women who use AI pay a competence penalty. In a study of more than 1,000 engineers reported by the Harvard Business Review, identical code was judged differently depending on who was known to have written it. Women who used AI saw their perceived competence drop by 13%, compared with 6% for men, and by 26% when the reviewers were men who did not use AI themselves. This is a digital version of the Matilda effect: When a woman uses the machine, the credit goes to the machine; when a man uses it, his judgment in choosing to use it is valued. Women are caught in a double bind: They are judged less competent if they use AI and less up to date if they don’t. 

4. Women are largely absent from one of today’s most lucrative industries. AI is already one of the best-paid segments of the market. According to LinkedIn, women accounted for only 26% of AI hires in 2025, compared with half of all hires in other sectors, and they hold only 13% of C-suite roles at AI companies. 

5. The tools are built mostly by men, and it shows. LLMs learn from data that reflects a world where men have long held the best jobs and earned the highest salaries. German researchers at the Technical University of Applied Sciences Würzburg-Schweinfurt asked chatbots for salary negotiation advice using profiles that were identical except for gender. Women were told to aim lower. In one case, the model suggested $280,000 for a woman and $400,000 for a man. Years earlier, Amazon had to drop an experimental recruiting tool after discovering it penalized CVs containing the word “women,” as in “women’s chess club captain.” The system had been trained on 10 years of applications, most of which came from men. In hiring, evaluation, and career advice, the same biases get repeated at scale.

6. New office chores replace the old ones. Someone still has to read the automated minutes, improve the AI-generated drafts, and catch the made-up figures and other hallucinations before they go out. AI slop takes time to process. I suspect a lot of this “cleanup” lands where office chores have always landed. If that’s right, some of the time saved by automating the old chores gets eaten by the new ones.

7. The jobs AI can’t do are the ones it watches most closely. Call centers and home care are good examples. In the U.S., 85% of home care workers are women, and since 2020, those paid through Medicaid have had to log every visit in an app that tracks them by GPS and checks their identity. Call center and retail workers know the same timed tasks and automated schedules. These women keep their jobs, but they lose more and more control over how they do them.

8. Deepfakes make visibility more dangerous for women. Nearly all deepfake videos online are pornographic, and 99% of the people targeted in them are women. Public life makes it worse: In the U.S. Congress, women were 70 times more likely than men to be targeted. Journalists, politicians, founders, and anyone whose career depends on being seen now face a risk men rarely do. Many women are likely to respond by stepping back—and who could blame them? After facing online abuse, 38% of women journalists surveyed by UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization) said they had lowered their public profile.

On balance

My list clearly has more negatives than positives, which in itself doesn’t mean much. Counting items doesn’t tell you how much each one weighs. Besides, the list is far from comprehensive. You may have other arguments on the credit or the debit side.

Still, having drawn up both columns, I would say the balance is negative for women’s work, at least for now. The main reason is a difference in timing. Most of the negatives are already happening: Women hold the most exposed jobs, the first rungs of the career ladder are disappearing, women who use AI are judged more harshly, they are a small minority in the sector where the money is, the tools carry biases, the jobs AI can’t do are increasingly monitored, and deepfakes make public visibility riskier.

Most of the positives, on the other hand, depend on conditions that haven’t yet been met: Greedy jobs will only loosen if firms deliberately redesign work, the time freed from office chores and paperwork can easily be swallowed by new tasks, and relational skills will only pay if employers finally choose to recognize them.

The balance could still shift, of course. What happens next will depend on choices made inside companies (about job design, evaluation, and hiring in AI) and on choices made at the ballot box (about how much public money goes to care).

items.title: [cloud.google.com] Google bans Chinese partner after backdoor infects 1.3 million Android boxes
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Google and security partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, which had enrolled more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes. Google says it has high confidence that Shenzhen-based manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co. deliberately embedded the backdoor in device firmware and sold criminal groups access to infected hardware. The criminal groups used the devices to commit advertising fraud, route other people’s internet traffic through household connections and install additional malware. Google also reported that operators captured screens, collected account information and system logs, and issued commands remotely. The same malware appeared on telehealth equipment, karaoke machines and digital signs. Google’s takedown targeted XCPE control servers and domains used by more than a dozen related malware families. Google estimates the takedown could also cut criminal access to at least 10 million other devices compromised through separate routes. Videostrong evaded Google’s device checks by loading malicious code after a device’s first boot, Google said. Google has banned Videostrong and its future affiliates from making certified Android devices or supplying software to certified manufacturers, and says it changed its review process. The backdoor remains in affected devices and can reinstall after a reboot. Synthient, a security firm involved in the investigation, recommends disconnecting and replacing affected boxes.

items.title: [efeagro.com] Hackers raise supermarket freezer temperatures across Europe, spoiling food
items.content_html: Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation, but no group has claimed responsibility and authorities have not established whether the incidents were part of one operation. Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.title: [tagesanzeiger.ch] Anthropic IPO filing discloses $161 billion in Broadcom chip commitments
items.content_html: Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, has disclosed five-year equipment lease agreements with semiconductor company Broadcom worth $161 billion as it seeks a stock-market listing. The commitments would make Anthropic Broadcom’s biggest customer for custom AI accelerator chips next year, according to Anthropic’s IPO filing and a Nov. 2 analysis. Anthropic is targeting a November listing, with reports placing the likely window in the week of Nov. 16. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan helped secure banks for a $63 billion chip-sale financing arrangement. The lenders plan to sell the debt in bond markets next year, exposing it to potential interest-rate increases. Anthropic’s filing, published after it submitted registration documents on Oct. 26, reports $16.3 billion in first-half revenue. Ed Elson, co-host of the Prof G Markets podcast, cautioned that investors may be underestimating how quickly Anthropic’s computing costs could rise. The company could spend as much as $150 billion on compute next year, compared with $8.9 billion in the first half of 2026, he said.
